Wild Camping in England and Wales: The Legal Reality

Unlike Scotland, wild camping in England and Wales is generally illegal without the landowner's permission. However, the reality is more nuanced than the law suggests, and there are legitimate ways to camp wild if you know the rules and the culture.

The Legal Position

In England and Wales, all land is owned by someone. Camping without permission is technically trespass — a civil offence, not a criminal one. This means:

  • You can't be arrested for wild camping (unless you refuse to leave when asked)
  • A landowner can ask you to move, and you must comply
  • If you leave no trace and cause no damage, prosecution is virtually unheard of
  • The key is being respectful, discreet, and responsible

Dartmoor: The Exception

Dartmoor National Park has a long-standing right of wild camping on open moorland, making it unique in England. Following a 2023 court case and subsequent legal clarification, camping is permitted on designated areas of the moor subject to conditions:

  • Camp on open moorland only, not in car parks or near roads
  • Small groups (1-2 tents)
  • Maximum 2 nights in one spot
  • Leave no trace
  • No fires (use a stove only)

Where Wild Camping Is Tolerated

While not strictly legal, wild camping is widely tolerated in several areas of England and Wales:

  • Lake District fells: Camping above the highest enclosed land (roughly above the wall line) is traditionally tolerated. Valleys and lakeshores are not.
  • Snowdonia: High mountain camping is generally tolerated. The summit plateau of Cadair Idris and the Carneddau are popular wild camping areas.
  • Yorkshire Dales: Remote moorland camping is tolerated if discreet.
  • Northumberland: The Cheviot Hills and remote border areas are vast enough that discreet camping goes unnoticed.

The Touring Rider's Guide to Discreet Camping

If you choose to camp discreetly in tolerated areas:

  • Arrive late, leave early — this is the golden rule
  • Camp out of sight of roads and buildings
  • Use a small, discreet-coloured tent (green or brown, not bright orange)
  • No fires — ever. Use a camping stove only.
  • Leave absolutely no trace. Pack out every scrap of waste.
  • If asked to move by a landowner or ranger, do so politely and immediately
  • Never camp near livestock, especially during lambing season (March-May)
The unwritten code in England and Wales: camp discreetly, leave no trace, and nobody will bother you. The moment you make a mess, leave litter, or camp in an intrusive location, you ruin it for everyone who follows.

Legal Alternatives

If you want to camp legally and cheaply in England and Wales:

  • Ask the landowner: Knock on a farmhouse door and ask. You'll be surprised how often the answer is "sure, camp in that field." Sometimes they'll even bring you eggs for breakfast.
  • Nearly Wild Camping: An organisation connecting campers with landowners who offer basic, affordable camping on their land.
  • Britstops: A network of pubs, farms, and vineyards offering free overnight parking (originally for campervans but some welcome bike tourers).
  • Budget campsites: Many basic campsites charge as little as £5-10 per night for a motorcycle and tent.

The wild camping situation in England and Wales isn't as free as Scotland, but with the right approach, you can still enjoy overnight adventures under the stars — legally and respectfully. Read our Northumberland Motorcycle Routes: England's Wild North guide for more.

Dartmoor is the exception, with a right to wild camp on designated open moorland subject to conditions.
Camping is widely tolerated high on the Lake District fells, Snowdonia peaks, Yorkshire Dales and Northumberland if discreet.
Arrive late, leave early, use a dull-coloured tent, never light fires, and leave no trace.
Legal cheap options include asking farmers directly, Nearly Wild Camping and Britstops.

faq.q: Can I wild camp in England and Wales?
faq.a: Generally no, not without the landowner's permission. All land is owned by someone, and camping without consent is trespass, which is a civil rather than criminal matter. You cannot be arrested unless you refuse to leave when asked. In practice, if you leave no trace and cause no damage, prosecution is virtually unheard of.

Yes. Dartmoor National Park has a long-standing right to wild camp on designated areas of open moorland, confirmed after a 2023 court case and subsequent legal clarification. You must camp on open moorland only rather than car parks or roadsides, keep to small groups of one or two tents, stay a maximum of two nights, light no fires and use a stove only.

faq.q: Where is wild camping tolerated even if not strictly legal?
faq.a: Discreet camping high on the Lake District fells above the wall line, on Snowdonia peaks such as Cadair Idris and the Carneddau, on remote Yorkshire Dales moorland, and in the Cheviot Hills of Northumberland is traditionally tolerated. Valleys and lakeshores are not. The unwritten rule is arrive late, leave early, and remain out of sight of roads and buildings.

Ask a farmer directly, as many will happily let you pitch in a field. Nearly Wild Camping connects campers with landowners offering basic, affordable sites. Britstops lists pubs, farms and vineyards offering free overnight parking, and basic campsites often charge just £5-10 per night for a motorcycle and tent.
